Social media marketing is simply using social platforms to help the right people find your business, trust it and buy from it. The first decision is not what to post. It is **where** to post. Every platform has a different crowd, a different style of content and different business tools. A small business with one or two people cannot do all of them well, so the skill is choosing.
Start with your customer, not the app

Before you look at any platform, write one sentence about your best customer: who she is, where she lives, what she needs and how she likes to buy. For example: "Working mothers in Lagos aged 28 to 45 who want ready-to-cook soup ingredients delivered on Saturday." This sentence is your **target audience**. Every choice in this course goes back to it.
**Who:** age range, gender if it matters, job or life stage
**Where:** city or area you can actually deliver to or serve
**Need:** the problem your product or service solves for her
**Buying habit:** does she buy after seeing photos, after chatting, after watching a demo, or after a friend recommends you?

Notice that WhatsApp is different from the rest. Facebook, Instagram and TikTok help people **discover** you. WhatsApp is where most Nigerian small businesses **close** the sale: the customer asks the price, sends a delivery address and confirms payment. The one main, one support rule

Pick **one main platform** where you post regularly and learn deeply, and **one support platform** where you share the best of the same content. Add WhatsApp Business as your sales channel. Only add a third platform when the first two run smoothly every week. Posting once a month on five platforms looks abandoned; posting four times a week on one looks alive.

Worked example: choosing platforms for a small catering business

For example, Funmi runs a small-chops and party-tray business in Ibadan. Her best customers are women aged 30 to 55 who organise birthdays, church events and office parties. She has one phone and about 5 hours a week for marketing.
She writes her customer sentence: "Event organisers in Ibadan who want reliable, tasty small chops delivered on time."
She notes her customers mostly ask friends for recommendations and look at photos of past events before ordering.
She chooses Facebook as her main platform, because her customers are active in local Facebook groups and she can post event photos and reviews there.
She chooses Instagram as her support platform and shares the same photos and short videos there, linked to Facebook through Meta Business Suite so one post can go to both.
She puts her WhatsApp Business link on both profiles so every enquiry lands in one inbox.
Funmi spends her 5 hours on two connected platforms instead of five, and all her orders arrive in one WhatsApp inbox she can track.
Questions to test your choice
Can I create the kind of content this platform rewards at least three times a week? TikTok needs video; LinkedIn needs written ideas; Instagram needs good pictures.
Do my customers use this platform to buy, or only to be entertained?
Can I reply to messages on it every day, or will enquiries be missed?
Does it have tools I need, such as a catalogue, scheduling or local ads?

If you answer "no" to two or more of these for a platform, it is probably not your main platform yet. You can still reserve your business name on it so nobody else takes it, and come back later when you have more time or help.

Search for three businesses like yours in your city. Note which platform gets them the most comments and real questions, not just likes. That is a strong clue about where your buyers are.

Worked example: rewriting a weak bio
For example, Ada sells ready-made Ankara dresses from her home in Abuja. Her old Instagram bio said: "God's own designer. Blessed. DM for enquiries."
She switches her Instagram to a Business account and picks the category "Clothing (brand)".
She changes her name field to "Ada's Ankara | Abuja" so it appears in searches for Ankara and Abuja.
She rewrites the bio: "Ready-to-wear Ankara dresses for work and owambe. Sizes 8 to 20. Delivery across Abuja. Order on WhatsApp below."
She adds her wa.me link and creates three Story Highlights: Price list, Reviews, How to order.
In WhatsApp Business she adds 12 dresses to the catalogue with prices and a greeting message: "Thank you for contacting Ada's Ankara. Send the dress name and your size."
A visitor now knows what Ada sells, for whom, in which sizes, where she delivers and exactly how to order, without asking a single question first.
Common profile mistakes to fix today
**Different names on every platform.** Use the same name and, if possible, the same handle everywhere so customers can find you and trust that it is really you.
**No prices anywhere.** You do not have to list every price, but a "from" price or a price list Highlight saves time and filters out people who cannot afford you.
**Out-of-date information.** Old phone numbers, closed shop addresses and expired offers make you look inactive. Check your profiles on the first day of each month.
**A private account.** A business account must be public so that new people can see your posts.

Ask a friend who has never seen your page to look at it for ten seconds, then tell you what you sell, where and how to order. If they cannot answer all three, your profile still needs work. This simple test is one of the fastest ways to find gaps you cannot see yourself.
Protect your accounts

Turn on two-factor authentication on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and WhatsApp. Never share login codes with anyone who messages you, even if they claim to be Meta support or offer you a verified badge. Account takeovers of Nigerian business pages often start with a fake support message.
Use quick replies
In WhatsApp Business, save quick replies for your price list, delivery fees and payment details. Typing a slash brings them up, which saves time and keeps your answers consistent.

How the feeds decide who sees your posts
Explain in plain words what a ranking algorithm does
Name the main signals Facebook, Instagram and TikTok use to rank content
Identify actions that help or hurt your reach

An **algorithm** is the set of rules an app uses to decide which posts to show each person, and in what order. Every user could see thousands of posts each day, so the app ranks them and shows what it predicts that person is most likely to watch, like, comment on or share. Nobody outside the companies knows the exact formulas, and they change often. But Meta and TikTok have both published explanations of the general signals they use, and those are worth understanding.
The signals, in plain words
**Your relationship with the viewer:** people who have messaged, commented on or watched you before are more likely to see you again.
**How people react to the post:** early watching, comments, shares and saves tell the app the post is worth showing to more people.
**Information about the post:** what it is about, when it was posted, whether it is a video, photo or text, and its caption and sounds.
**The viewer's own habits:** if she usually watches Reels about cooking, she is shown more cooking.

TikTok works a little differently from Facebook. Its **For You** feed mainly recommends videos based on what each person watches and interacts with, so a new account with few followers can still reach many people if a video holds attention. On Facebook and Instagram, followers and past interaction matter more for regular feed posts, while Reels are also recommended to people who do not follow you.

Worked example: reading what the feed is telling you

For example, Halima sells home-made zobo and tiger-nut drinks in Kaduna. In one week she posts three things on Instagram: a flyer with prices, a carousel of "5 ways to serve zobo at a party", and a 15-second Reel of her pouring chilled zobo over ice.
She opens Insights for each post after three days.
The flyer reached about 120 accounts with 2 saves. The carousel reached about 400 accounts with 35 saves. The Reel reached about 1,900 accounts, mostly non-followers, with 14 shares.
She notes the carousel was saved because it was useful, and the Reel travelled because it was visual and short.
She decides to post one useful carousel and two short Reels each week, and to put prices in a pinned post and a Highlight instead of daily flyers.
Halima stops guessing. She uses her own Insights to see which formats the feed rewards for her audience and plans more of those.
Turning signals into a posting habit

You cannot control the algorithm, but you can control what you give it. Three habits work across all platforms. First, **make every post easy to react to**: ask a real question in the caption, such as "Which colour would you wear to a wedding?", rather than "Comment YES". Second, **stay around after posting**. Spend 10 to 15 minutes replying to the first comments, because early conversation is a positive signal. Third, **make the first moment count**: the first line of a caption and the first seconds of a video decide whether people stop.

Also remember that each platform keeps adjusting how it ranks posts. When reach drops suddenly for a week, do not panic or delete posts. Check whether your posting pattern or content changed, look at what is working for similar accounts, and keep testing for at least two or three weeks before drawing conclusions.
Do not chase every rumour
You will hear claims like "post exactly at 7 pm" or "links kill your reach". Treat them as ideas to test, not rules. Your own Insights after a few weeks are more reliable than any general tip.
Never buy followers

Bought followers do not buy from you, and they do not react to your posts. Because the app first shows your post to some followers, fake ones make every post look unpopular and can reduce reach. They also break platform rules.

**Organic growth** means growing without paying for ads. It is slower than paid ads, but it builds a group of people who know and trust you, and it costs time rather than money. The method is simple: post useful content consistently, make it easy for the right people to find you, and talk to people as a human being.

Be easy to find
**Keywords:** people now search on Instagram and TikTok like a search engine. Put words like "Ankara dresses Abuja" in your name field, bio and captions.
**Hashtags:** use a few specific ones (for example #AbujaFashion, #LagosCaterer) rather than 30 general ones. Specific tags reach people who are actually looking.
**Location tags:** tag your city or area on posts, especially if you deliver locally.

Grow with other people

**Collaborations:** Instagram's Collab feature lets one post appear on two accounts. Partner with a business that serves the same customer but does not compete, for example a caterer and a cake maker.
**Groups:** join local Facebook groups where your customers ask for recommendations. Follow each group's rules, answer questions helpfully, and only promote where it is allowed.
**Customer content:** ask happy customers to post and tag you. Reshare with their permission.
**WhatsApp Status and Channels:** share new posts to your Status so existing contacts see them.
Worked example: a realistic weekly plan
For example, Chioma runs a small skincare shop in Port Harcourt that sells shea butter blends. She has about 4 hours a week and uses Instagram as her main platform and Facebook as support.
Sunday (1 hour): she batches content. She films two Reels and takes photos for a carousel in one session.
Monday: a Teach carousel, "How to store shea butter in Port Harcourt heat", posted to Instagram and Facebook together through Business Suite.
Wednesday: a Show the work Reel of her whipping a batch, with the caption keyword "whipped shea butter Port Harcourt".
Friday: a Proof post sharing a customer review with permission, plus an Offer line at the end with her WhatsApp link.
Every day (15 minutes): she replies to comments and messages and spends 5 minutes commenting helpfully in two local groups.
Chioma posts three times a week, every week, in about 4 hours. After a month she compares follower growth and the number of WhatsApp enquiries that mention Instagram.
A growth routine you can keep

Growth comes from small actions repeated every week. Many small business owners post and leave, then wonder why nothing happens. Social platforms are built around conversation, so the owner who comments, answers and shows up daily grows faster than the one who only posts.
Before posting, spend 5 minutes replying to comments on your last post.
After posting, stay for 10 minutes to answer early comments and messages.
Leave thoughtful comments on 5 posts from local customers, partners or groups (real sentences, not just emojis).
Share the new post to your WhatsApp Status and, where allowed, one relevant group.
Once a week, reshare a customer review or tagged post with permission.
Done three times a week, this routine takes about 30 minutes each time and builds relationships that turn into referrals and repeat orders.
Measure enquiries, not just followers

Ask every new customer "Where did you hear about us?" and tally the answers in a notebook. A page with 800 followers that brings ten orders a month is doing better than one with 8,000 followers that brings none.
Respect privacy

Always ask before posting a customer's photo, name or chat screenshot, and blur phone numbers and addresses. Under Nigeria's Data Protection Act, personal data should be used fairly and with a lawful basis such as consent.

Writing captions that sell

A strong caption has three parts. The **hook** is the first line, the only part people see before tapping "more", so it must make them want to read on. The **value** is the useful middle: details, benefits, a short story or tips. The **call to action** (CTA) tells them exactly what to do next: "Send 'TRAY' on WhatsApp to get the price list", "Save this for your next party", "Tag a friend who is planning a wedding".
Weak hook: "Good morning everyone." Strong hook: "Your jollof is not watery because of the rice. It is the tomatoes."
Write the way you speak to a customer. Short sentences. Simple words. Pidgin or local language is fine if your customers use it.
Mention price ranges or "from" prices where you can. Many buyers skip posts that only say "DM for price".
Use one CTA per post. Two or three CTAs confuse people.

Plan, batch and schedule

A **content calendar** is a simple table of what you will post and when. Plan a week or a month at once, create the photos and videos in one or two sessions (called batching), then schedule them. In **Meta Business Suite**, use Create post or Create reel, choose your Facebook Page and Instagram account, then pick Schedule instead of Publish now. The Planner view shows everything you have scheduled. TikTok also offers scheduling in its web tools for eligible accounts.
Worked example: one product, three formats
For example, Bisi makes adire tote bags in Abeokuta and sells them from 15,000 naira (approximate). She wants to launch a new indigo design this week.
Monday (discover): a 12-second Reel of the bag being unfolded and packed with a laptop and water bottle. Hook on screen: "Fits a 14-inch laptop."
Wednesday (trust): a carousel of 6 slides: the dye process, the stitching, inside pockets, a customer carrying it, size details, and the CTA slide.

Accessibility and clarity

Many people scroll in noisy buses, quiet offices or with poor eyesight. Make your posts easy for everyone: use large text with strong contrast (dark text on light backgrounds or the reverse), avoid putting important words over busy photos, and add alt text to images in Instagram and Facebook under advanced or accessibility settings. Write emojis sparingly, because screen readers read every one aloud.

Check every post on your own phone before publishing. Is the price readable? Is the product clearly the main subject? Is the call to action obvious? Would a customer who has never heard of you understand it in three seconds? If not, simplify. Fewer words and one clear picture almost always beat a crowded design. Finally, keep a simple folder on your phone for each week's photos and videos, named by date, so you can find and reuse your best content later.

Reels on Instagram and Facebook and videos on TikTok are recommended to people who do not follow you, which makes them your best organic way to reach new customers. You do not need a camera crew. A clean phone lens, good light and a plan are enough.
The 3-part video plan

**Hook (first 1 to 3 seconds):** show the most interesting moment or say a bold line. "Watch this plain fabric become a wedding gown." Many viewers decide to keep watching or scroll within the first seconds.
**Body (5 to 40 seconds):** show the process, the result or the tip. Cut out any waiting. Each shot should be short.
**Call to action (last 2 to 3 seconds):** tell people what to do: "Order on WhatsApp, link in bio."

Filming basics
Wipe the phone lens with a soft cloth. Fingerprints make video look foggy.
Film vertically (phone upright) for Reels, TikTok and Stories.
Face a window or film outside in shade. Avoid strong light behind you, which turns you into a shadow. A ring light helps at night.
Keep the phone steady: rest it on a stack of books, a tripod or against a wall.
Record sound close to the speaker. A cheap clip-on microphone improves voice a lot. If it is noisy, add captions and music instead of speaking.
Film more short clips than you need, 3 to 5 seconds each, so editing is easy.
Editing and posting

You can edit inside the Instagram or TikTok app, or use **CapCut**, which has a free version. Add on-screen text for the hook, auto-captions so people can follow with the sound off, and music. Use music from the app's own library, because copyrighted songs added from elsewhere can get your video muted or blocked, and business accounts often have a more limited commercial music library. Choose a cover image that shows the product clearly, because it appears on your profile grid.
Worked example: a product demo Reel
For example, Esther sells blenders and kitchen gadgets from a small shop in Onitsha. She wants a video that shows her best-selling blender is strong enough for tiger nuts.
Hook (2 seconds): close-up of hard dry tiger nuts poured into the jar, text on screen: "Can it blend tiger nuts?"
Body (12 seconds): four 3-second clips: lid closing, blender running, smooth milk being poured through a sieve, a glass of tiger-nut milk.
CTA (3 seconds): text: "Available in Onitsha. Delivery across Anambra. WhatsApp link in bio."
She edits in CapCut, adds auto-captions and a track from the app library, and posts to Instagram as a Reel shared to Facebook.
She downloads the version without the Instagram watermark from CapCut and posts it separately on TikTok and her WhatsApp Status.
One 17-second video, filmed in 20 minutes, now works on four channels and answers the question customers ask most.
Reading your video results

Video analytics tell you exactly where people lose interest. On TikTok and in Instagram Reels Insights, look at **average watch time** and, where shown, the **retention graph** that shows how many viewers are still watching at each second. A sharp drop in the first two seconds means your hook is weak. A slow fade in the middle means the body is too long or repetitive. Lots of replays mean the video is satisfying or useful to watch again.
Low views and low watch time: improve the hook and the cover image.
Good watch time but few profile visits: add a clearer reason to visit, such as "See prices in my bio".
Many shares: make more videos on the same topic; people find it worth passing on.
Many comments asking the same question: answer it in your next video.
Give each video a few days before judging it, and compare it with your own past videos, not with famous creators.
Keep your raw clips after posting. A 30-second video can later become a 7-second teaser, a Story, or part of an ad, so a folder of good clips saves hours of filming.
Video ideas that never run out
Answer one customer question per video. Show before and after. Show packing an order. Compare two products. Show a common mistake and the fix. Each of these can be filmed in under 30 minutes.
Do not repost with another app's watermark
Post the clean file from your editor on each platform. Videos carrying a visible watermark from a different app may be shown to fewer people.

**Community management** means looking after the people who interact with your business online: replying to comments, answering messages, handling complaints and encouraging conversation. For a small business, this is where most sales are actually won. A customer who asks "How much?" and waits two days for a reply often buys from someone else.
Reply in a way that sells
**Answer the question first.** If someone asks the price, give the price or price range. Then invite the next step.
**Use their name** and keep a warm, respectful tone.
**Move buying conversations to private chat:** "The medium size is 12,000 naira (approximate). I have sent you photos on WhatsApp."
**Reply to every genuine comment,** even with a short thank you. Replies create conversation, which helps the post reach more people.
**Pin helpful comments** or your own comment with ordering details.

Use the **Meta Business Suite inbox** to answer Facebook and Instagram messages and comments in one place, and set automatic replies such as an instant greeting and FAQs. In **WhatsApp Business**, use **labels** (for example New enquiry, Awaiting payment, Paid, Delivered) so you can see where every customer is. Save **quick replies** for your price list, delivery fees and account details. Set an **away message** for outside working hours that says when you will reply.

Handling complaints and negative comments
Do not delete honest complaints or argue in public. Other customers are watching how you respond.
Reply quickly and calmly in public: thank them, apologise for the experience, and invite them to private chat to solve it.
In private, listen, ask for the order details, and offer a fair fix: replacement, repair, partial refund or credit.
When it is solved, it is fine to reply publicly that it has been resolved.
Do hide or delete spam, insults, scams and comments that share private information, and block repeat abusers.
Worked example: rescuing a public complaint
For example, Amaka runs a cake business in Enugu. A customer comments under her latest post: "My cake arrived with the top crushed. Very disappointing."
Within an hour, Amaka replies publicly: "I am so sorry, Nkechi. That is not the standard we aim for. I have sent you a message so we can make this right today."
In WhatsApp she asks for a photo, the order date and the delivery time, and learns the rider was delayed in traffic for two hours on a hot afternoon.
She offers a free replacement cake for the next week or a 50 percent refund. Nkechi chooses the replacement.
Amaka changes her delivery process: insulated boxes and no cake deliveries left in vehicles for long periods.
After the replacement, Nkechi updates her comment to say the issue was resolved.
A public complaint became public proof of good service, and Amaka fixed the real cause so it does not happen again.
Building a community, not just a customer list

Customers who feel part of something come back and bring friends. Simple ways to build that feeling: celebrate customers (with permission) in a weekly "customer of the week" post, ask for opinions before launching new products, reply to Stories that mention you, and thank repeat customers by name. A WhatsApp Channel or a small Facebook Group for loyal customers can share early access to new stock or special offers.

Write down your house rules for comments, for example no insults, no spam links, no sharing other people's private information. Pin them if you run a group. Clear rules make it easier to remove abuse fairly and keep the space pleasant for everyone. Also decide who answers messages when you are ill, travelling or busy; even a trusted family member with saved quick replies is better than silence for days.

Measure your service as well as your posts. Each week, note how many enquiries you received, how quickly you replied on average, and how many enquiries became orders. If many people ask the price and then go silent, test sending photos and the delivery fee together in your first reply, or offering two clear options instead of one. Small changes in how you reply often lift sales more than new posts do.
Set a response time and keep it
Decide on a reply time you can keep, for example within 2 hours between 8 am and 8 pm. Put your hours in your profile and away message. Consistent replies build trust faster than clever posts.
Protect customer data
Never post a customer's phone number, address or payment details in comments. Use private chat for anything personal, and do not share chat screenshots without blurring personal information.

**Promote proven content.** Pay to push a post that is already getting comments, shares or saves organically. Ads amplify; they rarely rescue a weak post.

**Targeting all of Nigeria when you only deliver in one city.** You pay for messages you cannot serve.

Hooks that work for ads
The first line of primary text and the first seconds of video do most of the work. Here are hook patterns you can adapt honestly to your own business:
**Question:** "Still washing your curtains by hand every month?"
**Specific promise:** "Your wedding small chops, delivered hot in Ibadan, on time."
**Before and after:** show the problem, then the result.
**Customer voice:** a short real review read aloud or shown on screen, with permission.
**Myth buster:** "Shea butter does not go bad in two weeks. Here is how to store it."

Write five hooks for each new ad and test the best two. Keep a swipe file, a folder of your best-performing ads and other ads you admire from the Ad Library, so you never start from a blank page. Remember that ad creative wears out: when the same audience has seen an ad many times, results drop, and a fresh video with a new hook often brings costs back down.

Before publishing, preview your ad in every placement Ads Manager offers, such as Facebook Feed, Instagram Feed, Stories and Reels. Text that looks fine in the feed may be covered by buttons in Stories. If a placement looks wrong, upload a version made for that size or remove that placement. Also read your ad copy aloud once: if it sounds like a radio jingle rather than a person talking to a friend, simplify it.

You do not need a big budget to learn from ads, but you do need to control spending and measure results. The question is never "How much should I spend?" alone. It is "How much can I afford to pay to get one customer, and is the ad getting customers below that amount?"
Budget types
**Daily budget:** the average amount spent per day. Meta may spend a bit more on some days and less on others, but keeps the weekly total in line with your daily budget.
**Lifetime budget:** a total amount over a set period, for example 15,000 naira (approximate) from Monday to Sunday. Useful for a promotion with an end date.
**Minimum budget:** Ads Manager shows the minimum allowed for your currency and objective when you set the budget, so check it there rather than relying on a figure you heard.

Meta explains that ad sets usually need around 50 results in a week to leave learning. Results can be unstable during this time, so avoid editing the ad every day. Small budgets may stay in learning; that is normal, so judge them over a week rather than a day.

For example, Rukayat sells ready-to-cook pepper soup packs in Lagos for about 6,500 naira (approximate). After ingredients, packaging and her own delivery cost, she keeps about 2,500 naira profit per pack.
She runs a Click-to-WhatsApp ad at about 2,000 naira per day for 7 days: total spend about 14,000 naira.

Cost per order = 14,000 ÷ 10 = 1,400 naira. Her break-even is 2,500 naira, so each order still leaves about 1,100 naira profit after ads.

Worked example: a monthly review
For example, Zainab sells handmade beaded jewellery in Kano through Instagram and WhatsApp. At the end of the month she reviews her 12 posts.

Keep a simple tracking sheet

Understanding your audience data

Insights also tell you **who** your followers are: top cities, age ranges, gender and the times they are most active. Compare this with your customer sentence from Lesson 1.1. If your buyers are mostly 30 to 45 but your followers are mostly 18 to 24, adjust your content style, topics and partners.

Use the "most active times" chart as a starting point for when to post, then test two or three time slots for a few weeks and keep the one that gives the best results. Look too at which posts brought **new followers**, because those topics are the ones introducing you to fresh people.

Finally, check the trend, not just the total. Is reach growing month by month? Are more enquiries coming from social media than three months ago? A steady upward trend matters more than one viral post.
**Weekly (10 minutes):** check messages answered, enquiries and orders in your sheet.
**Monthly (1 hour):** review Insights, ad results and the sheet together, then write three decisions.
**Quarterly:** compare the three months with your goals and update your plan (Lesson 4.4).
Screenshots help too. Save a screenshot of your account overview on the first day of each month, so you can compare months even if the app changes how it displays data.

**Audience fit:** do their followers live where you sell and look like your customer? Ask for a screenshot of their audience Insights (top cities, age, gender).

The brief and the agreement

Write down what you agreed, even for a small deal: deliverables (for example one Reel and three Stories), dates, key messages, what must not be said (such as health claims), whether you can reuse the content in ads, payment amount and timing, and how results will be tracked. A simple tracking method is a special discount code or a phrase like "Tell us Tolu sent you" so you can count orders.
Worked example: a micro-influencer deal
For example, Ifeoma runs a small bakery in Owerri. A local food reviewer with about 15,000 followers, mostly in Imo State, offers a Reel and Stories for 40,000 naira (approximate).
Ifeoma checks the last 10 Reels: typical views are 8,000 to 12,000 with real comments asking where to buy.
She asks for audience Insights; most followers are in Owerri and aged 22 to 40.
They agree in writing: one Reel and three Stories, the bakery tagged with the Paid partnership label, code "OWERRI10" for 10 percent off, half paid before posting and half after.
Over two weeks, 22 orders use the code, averaging 9,000 naira (approximate) each, about 198,000 naira in sales.

Paying and measuring fairly

Common ways to pay creators are a fixed fee per post, free products in exchange for honest content (often called gifting), a commission on each sale through their code, or a mix such as a small fee plus commission. For a first test, a mix reduces your risk and rewards the creator for real results. Agree the payment method and dates in writing and pay on time; creators talk to each other, and a good reputation brings better partners.

Measure every partnership the same way: how many people used the code or mentioned the partner, how many orders and how much revenue came in, and what you paid. Divide total cost by orders to get your cost per order, exactly as you did for ads in Lesson 3.4. Compare partners with each other and with ads, and keep working with those who bring customers at a cost you can afford. Long-term relationships with a few reliable creators usually work better than one-off posts with many.

Start small. Test one creator with a modest deal before signing a longer agreement, and agree in advance what happens if the content is late, off-message or never posted. A clear, friendly brief protects both of you and makes the next collaboration easier. Keep copies of the final posts and your written agreement in one folder for future reference.

Instagram, Facebook and TikTok require paid content to be disclosed, using tools such as Instagram's Paid partnership label or TikTok's content disclosure setting. Honest disclosure also protects trust in both of you.

Getting a new customer through social media costs time and often money. Selling again to someone who already trusts you is much cheaper, so plan for repeat orders from the start.

**Send a thank-you message** after delivery with a care tip, for example how to wash an Ankara dress so the colours last.

Running your monthly review

Set a fixed date each month for your review, for example the last Saturday, and give it one hour. Open your tracking sheet, Insights and Ads Manager. Answer five questions in writing: Did we reach our goals for the month? Which three posts brought the most enquiries or orders? Which platform or format took time but brought little? What did ads cost per order compared with break-even? What will we do more of, less of, and try new next month?

Turn the answers into three clear decisions, such as "two Proof posts a week instead of one", "pause the Facebook interest ad" and "test one TikTok video a week". Write them at the top of next month's calendar. At the end of 90 days, compare your results with the goals you set at the start, celebrate what improved, and write the next 90-day plan using what you have learned about your own customers. Over a year, four cycles of plan, act, measure and adjust will teach you more about your market than any general advice.

Share your plan with anyone who helps you, such as a family member who packs orders or a friend who films videos, so everyone knows the posting days, the offers coming up and how quickly customers must be answered. A plan that lives only in your head is easy to forget during a busy week; a written one on the wall or in your phone keeps the whole team on track.

Value: details, benefits, a short story

A strong caption has three parts. The hook is the first line, the only part people see before tapping more. Good morning everyone is weak. Your jollof is not watery because of the rice, it is the tomatoes, is strong.

Worked example

Here is the most important calculation in this module. Rukayat sells pepper soup packs in Lagos.
Each pack sells for about 6,500 naira. After ingredients, packaging and delivery she keeps about 2,500 naira. That is her break-even cost per order. Ads must cost less than this.
